item.title: WATCH: Heartwarming update on Punch the Monkey
item.description: The baby macaque at Japan’s Ichikawa City Zoo became a viral sensation after turning to an IKEA toy for comfort. Nine months later, Punch has joined the troop and taken an interest in a baby macaque.

item.title: WATCH: Empire State Building climbers appear in court
item.description: The daredevil couple who were arrested after climbing to the top of the Empire State Building were in court on Thursday to face criminal charges and possible deportation.

item.title: Iran live updates: US denies Iran's claim that it destroyed US radar in Bahrain
item.description: President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28.

item.title: Roger Waters launches heartfelt plea for 'an end to the genocide in Gaza'
item.description: Pink Floyd co-founder Roger Waters has always mixed art with activism. A long-standing supporter of the Palestinian cause, the star guitarist has now released a re-imagined version of the rock anthem "Comfortably Numb" with Palestinian American singer Mona Miari singing in Arabic. He tells FRANCE 24's Lyana Saleh why proceeds of the record are going to the Palestine Children's Relief Fund and why he can never become "Comfortably Numb" with the violence and suffering in Gaza.

item.title: 'Devastated wasteland': Haitian security forces regain control of stadium from gangs
item.description: Haitian security forces said they have regained control of the country's main stadium, wresting it back from the gangs that have been using it for the past two years. They were assisted by the Task Force, a private security group serving the government. The stadium is now under the guard of Salvadoran soldiers. FRANCE 24's senior reporter Catherine Norris Trent, who has covered Haiti extensively, said re-taking the stadium would be a significant step in an area of the city that had been a "devastated wasteland".

item.title: The truth about Douma: How Syria covered up a chemical attack
item.description: On April 7, 2018, the Syrian town of Douma, on the outskirts of the capital Damascus, was targeted by a chemical attack. Evidence pointed to the Syrian regime, yet proof vanished, and eyewitnesses went silent. Eight years later, FRANCE 24's Jenna Le Bras tracked down survivors and witnesses of the deadly attack. She also met representatives of some of the world's most powerful institutions to understand how a massive cover-up campaign had been orchestrated by the regime, with Russian support.

item.title: What does the 'Blue Tsunami' mean for US media?
item.description: This week, FRANCE 24's media show Scoop looks at the impact of the midterm elections in the United States. While the results are being reckoned with by Republicans and celebrated by Democrats, what does it all mean for the press? Some media analysts wonder whether certain outlets, particularly ones accused of being cosy with the Trump administration, will change their tone. Our guest this week is International Affairs Commentator Douglas Herbert.

item.title: Most Ukrainians 'think there's no chance of a peace deal' with Russia
item.description: Ukrainian attacks killed at least nine people in Russia overnight, while Moscow struck a hospital in Kyiv and killed at least three in the south of the country, officials on both sides said Friday. It comes a day after intense shuttle diplomacy in US-led talks to end the war approaching its fifth year but, says France 24's correspondent in Kyiv Gulliver Cragg, most people in Ukraine think there is "no chance" of a peace deal being reached.

item.title: 'A lot of emotion' as Paris marks 11 years since terror attacks
item.description: France on Friday marked 11 years since the November 13, 2015, terror attacks that left more than 130 dead in the capital. France 24's James André reports from outside the Bataclan concert venue, one of the sites targeted in the attacks, where he says there was "a lot of emotion" as homage was paid to the victims.

item.title: WATCH: SS United States sinks off of Florida coast to become artificial reef
item.description: The ocean liner, larger than the Titanic, was sunk into the ocean to create the world's largest artificial reef.

item.title: UK rocked by comedians' sex scandals
item.description: The UK is facing a reckoning in the world of entertainment, as two well-known comedy figures find themselves at the centre of serious allegations and headlines. This as Russell Brand is jailed for more than 10 years after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault and David Walliams faces serious allegations of sexual misconduct.

item.title: Republicans dazed by midterm election defeats grapple with what went wrong
item.description: Republicans are grappling with unexpected losses after the midterm elections

item.description: Mauricio Pochettino is out as head coach of the U.S. men's national soccer team. Pochettino led the U.S. to the round of 16 at last year's World Cup. He's departing to coach Manchester United.

item.title: The scourge of femicide in Mexico: Impunity reigns in state of Morelos
item.description: When Claudia Sheinbaum became Mexico's first female president in 2024, she pledged to tackle violence against women. And while femicides have fallen since she took office, the numbers remain alarming, with around 520 murders so far this year. In the small state of Morelos, just outside the capital Mexico City, four female students have been murdered since January, including a Spanish woman on an exchange programme. The state has one of the highest femicide rates in the country.

item.title: Temperatures drop to -6C with cold weather alert in force in some areas
item.description: Temperatures dropped below -6C overnight as parts of the country remain under a cold weather health alert.

item.title: Ukraine’s mobilisation methods spark criticism
item.description: Social media in Ukraine is full of videos showing suspected cases of forced mobilisation. Such incidents are known as “busification”, as the recruitment officers typically take the conscripts away in minibuses. The videos have been fuelling growing opposition to the recruitment practices.

item.title: Happy World Kindness Day! Check out our kind photos of kindness to humans -- and cats
item.description: Friday, November 13 is World Kindness Day. Your mission: Do something kind. Small acts of kindness definitely count!

item.title: Nvidia scandal: Was Alice Huang really a Chinese spy?
item.description: It is another twist in the downfall of Jensen Huang, CEO of AI chip giant Nvidia, who resigned on Thursday. The US Justice Department says it has not yet reached a conclusion on whether Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman he had an affair with, was a spy. CNN is also reporting sources from across the US intelligence community who say there is no definitive proof she was an intelligence asset for Beijing

item.title: It's 'game over' for Jensen Huang, king of AI chips
item.description: PRESS REVIEW – Friday, November 13: We look at reactions to the resignation of Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia. It comes in the wake of multiple affairs he allegedly had, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. What are the repercussions for the AI industry and for AI trade relations? Also: France's Les Bleus lose to Italy in the Nations League, marking Zinédine Zidane's first defeat as coach. Plus: a raccoon that went viral for getting drunk last year ends up raising a lot of money for an animal shelter!

item.title: Jeffrey Donaldson's wife Eleanor placed on sex offenders' register after his rape conviction
item.description: Eleanor Donaldson, the wife of disgraced former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson, has been placed on the sex offenders' register.

item.title: Haitian police retake national stadium after two years of gang control
item.description: Haitian security forces regained control of the country's main football stadium on Thursday, ending two years of gang control. Salvadoran troops have now taken over security at the venue. El Salvador deployed 2,000 soldiers to Haiti following an ambush in which four of its troops went missing.

item.title: Kratom and 7-OH can feel like 'a miracle.' They can also be addictive
item.description: In the last decade, strong support for kratom and 7-OH products have kept them federally legal. That's started to change. A crackdown for some highly potent products related to kratom is coming.

item.title: US, Ukraine say Europe to join peace talks as Putin sticks to hardline stance
item.description: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and US envoy Jared Kushner said Thursday, November 12, Europe would join the next round of talks with Russia, as Vladimir Putin indicated Moscow will not compromise on its hardline demands to end almost five years of war. In a packed day of shuttle diplomacy following negotiations in Abu Dhabi, Kushner and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff held over four hours of talks with Putin in the Kremlin before jetting to debrief Zelensky in Dublin.

item.title: Fallout from Nvidia scandal spreads as Huang resigns
item.description: Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of spying for China. The news wiped 4.3% of Nvidia’s share price by closing bell Thursday, while the scandal has also raised concerns over security in the United States, with the spotlight falling on US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

item.title: Peruvians flock to see Pope Leo XIV in city he served as bishop
item.description: Crowds in Peru's northern city of Chiclayo gathered early on Friday, November 13, ​ahead of ‌Pope Leo's arrival for the centerpiece event of his 12-day South America tour, an outdoor ⁠Mass with the people who called him their bishop for eight years. He declared on November 11 that the country where he served as a missionary for about 20 years was his homeland.

item.title: Microsoft faces a major Outlook outage: ‘no signs of a cyberattack’
item.description: Microsoft said "malicious" activity was not to blame for an Outlook outage that left users around the world without its crucial services on Friday, November 13, but reported making headway in fixing the massive disruption. Businesses, governments and likely millions of individuals have been without services like Outlook email for over half a day, triggering wide-ranging consequences.

item.title: France remembers victims of 2015 Paris terror attacks
item.description: France on Friday marks 11 years since the 2015 Paris terror attacks, in which more than 130 were killed as gunmen and suicide bombers attacked the Bataclan concert hall, a major stadium, restaurants and bars. France 24’s James André reports from outside the Bataclan where a tribute to the victims is being held.

item.title: Guinea opens illegal gold mining trial, 1,200 people arrested
item.description: Guinea opened a trial over illegal gold mining on Thursday, November 12, after a crackdown on mineral extraction in the district of Siguiri. There was a ban on "unregulated and illegal" gold mining in the area where the military was subsequently deployed. Security forces have expelled tens of thousands of foreign nationals who had come to work in the region's mines.

item.title: 'No war, no peace' situation between US and Iran 'cannot continue', Iraqi FM says
item.description: In an interview with FRANCE 24, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said the "no war and no peace" situation in the region "cannot continue". He also said that closing all but two border crossings with Iran, as Washington demands, was "not possible". Finally, he confirmed that Iraqi oil now is now flowing through the Strait of Hormuz under US protection.

item.title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who chastised him
item.description: Pete Hegseth was yelled at by a sentinel for poor decorum at Arlington National Cemetery. Now the Secretary of Defense has given him a medal.

item.title: Toera's homecoming: Madagascar's slain king joins his ancestors after 129 years
item.description: In 1897, French colonial troops killed King Toera, ruler of Madagascar's powerful Sakalava kingdom of Menabe, and took his skull to Paris, where it remained hidden in a museum for more than a century. France returned the remains last year, and for the first time since his death, King Toera took his place among his ancestors during the Sakalava people's most sacred ritual.

item.title: Amnesty criticises South Sudan, UN over failure to heed massacre warnings
item.description: Amnesty International said Thursday, November 12, that South Sudan and UN peacekeepers failed to act on warnings of a massacre that ended with more than 200 dead in March. The world's youngest country has been plagued by civil war, poverty, corruption and intercommunal violence since it was formed in 2011. FRANCE 24 spoke to Donatella Rovera, Senior crisis response adviser at Amnesty International.

item.title: 'Big development' in peace talks as Ukraine says Europe to join Russia negotiations
item.description: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and US envoy Jared Kushner said Thursday Europe would join the next round of talks with Russia, as Vladimir Putin indicated Moscow will not compromise on its hardline demands to end almost five years of war. Kushner and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff held over four hours of talks with Putin in the Kremlin before jetting to debrief Zelensky in Dublin. France 24's Andrew Hilliar has the details.

item.title: As world gripped by climate emergency, COP31’s empty chairs signal low ambitions
item.description: It is the recurring theme of every speech at the COP summits: the urgent need to act in the face of increasingly frequent climate disasters. Yet this year’s conference in Turkey seems to have little ambition, as reflected in the low turnout and the host country’s own contradictions. Morgan Ayre has the story.

item.title: Rivers in the sky are raining down on the Pacific Northwest. What are they?
item.description: Atmospheric rivers are large bands of water vapor in the sky. They are dumping trillions of gallons of water on Washington and Oregon, just as high tides and winds batter shorelines.

item.description: The forthcoming move has left some parents and educators frustrated and wondering about the company's motivations.
